tagline.text: 17,000 white crosses holding the memory of the Pacific War

location.label: Location
location.text: Fort Bonifacio, Taguig City, Metro Manila

image.credit: Elmer B. Domingo / CC BY-SA 3.0 / Wikimedia Commons

items.credit: Dan Lundberg / CC BY-SA 2.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A memorial park where more than 17,000 American and Filipino servicemen who died in the Pacific Theater of World War II rest, the largest overseas American cemetery from that war. Its endless rows of white marble crosses, the Walls of the Missing bearing over 36,000 names, and its vast mosaic battle maps quietly convey the weight of the war.

The Manila American Cemetery and Memorial sits in Fort Bonifacio, Taguig City, in Metro Manila, just south of the new town of BGC. Across roughly 61 gently rolling hectares of grass, tropical trees stand sparsely, with white marble headstones stretching out endlessly between them in concentric arcs. It's managed by the American Battle Monuments Commission (ABMC), a U.S. government agency, and admission is free for everyone.

There are 17,206 graves here in total. Most are American service members who died across New Guinea and the Philippines — in the Japanese invasion of the Philippines and the battles of Bataan and Corregidor in
, and the Leyte landings and the battle to retake Manila in

— and 570 Filipino soldiers, including Philippine Scouts who fought alongside American forces, also rest here. Some 3,700 graves belong to unknown soldiers whose names were never recovered. The cemetery began construction in
and was dedicated together with its memorial in

A chapel and memorial stand atop the hill at the center of the burial area, flanked by a semicircular colonnade that spreads out like two open arms. The walls of the colonnade bear the names of 36,286 missing whose remains were never found, and inside its rooms hang 25 large mosaic maps depicting the major battles of the Pacific War. This land was once the site of Fort William McKinley, a U.S. Army base, and it's now a quiet expanse of green at the heart of a city ringed by high-rises.

It's a rewarding stop for travelers interested in war history, and also a good choice for anyone staying in BGC or Makati who wants a quiet walk within the city. For Koreans, it offers a chance to look back on the same period of the Pacific War from a Philippine perspective, and it's a fitting place to talk with family about the meaning of peace.

Crosses of white Italian marble, along with Star of David headstones for Jewish service members, are laid out across eleven plots in concentric arcs. Looking down from the hill, the scene of grass, trees, and white headstones together is deeply moving.

The walls of the semicircular colonnade bear the names of 36,286 missing, along with their rank, unit, and home state. A small rosette beside a name marks someone whose remains were later recovered and identified.

The 25 mosaic maps hanging in the colonnade's four rooms use colored stone to depict battles from Pearl Harbor to Bataan, Leyte, the retaking of Manila, and Okinawa, across the Pacific and the China-Burma-India theater. You can also trace the course of fighting on fronts close to Korea.
At the center of the memorial, the chapel is a quiet space combining mosaic decoration with a high ceiling. Sit for a moment in silent reflection and remember those who rest here.
The names of the five Sullivan brothers, who died together when the cruiser USS Juneau sank in
, are inscribed side by side on the Walls of the Missing. This tragedy is known as the reason the U.S. military later stopped assigning brothers to the same unit.

570 Filipino soldiers, including Philippine Scouts who fought under American command, rest in the same burial ground as their American comrades — a reminder of the war the two nations fought together.
At the visitor center near the entrance, you can pick up cemetery guide materials and view exhibits. If you're looking for a specific grave or name, staff can help you locate it.

Enter "Manila American Cemetery and Memorial" as your destination. After an ID check at the entrance gate, vehicles can drive in to the visitor parking area. Calling a Grab to leave usually works well from inside the cemetery, but wait times can grow longer around sunset.
Take a BGC bus from a stop near MRT-3's Ayala station into BGC, then switch to a Grab or walk the rest of the way. The BGC bus fare is about
; routes and stops change often, so check before boarding.

The BGC Bus EDSA Ayala Terminal is at the corner of EDSA and McKinley Road, right next to the MRT Ayala station, and the East Express route runs to Market! Market!. rainy season, afternoon showers are frequent and the grass turns slippery when wet, so bring an umbrella and comfortable walking shoes. After the rain clears, the white headstones stand out sharply against the green grass under a cloudy sky, which can actually make for great photos. Around the memorial events in late May and on November 11, security is tightened and general visits may be restricted.

Since the cemetery sits right next to BGC, staying in BGC or Makati is most convenient. BGC has many international chain hotels (about
per night) and serviced residences (about
), and McKinley Hill, just south of the cemetery, also has condo-style accommodations. With the airport nearby, it's also a good place to stay the night before departure.

There's no restaurant or shop inside the cemetery, so bring water with you. After your visit, head to Venice Grand Canal Mall on McKinley Hill, about a 5–10 minute drive away, for a meal overlooking the canal, or go to the restaurant strips of BGC High Street and Uptown, where you'll find everything from Filipino food to Korean, Japanese, and Western cuisine. For something quick and cheap, the food court at Market! Market! mall has affordable Filipino rice bowls, grilled skewers, and the dessert halo-halo.
You may be asked for ID at the entrance, so bring a passport or another photo ID.
You'll be walking a fair amount across lawns and hills. Bring a hat, sunscreen, water, and comfortable shoes.

If you're looking for a specific veteran, use the search function on the American Battle Monuments Commission's website beforehand to find the plot and row number — it makes finding the grave much easier.

Pairing this with a BGC or Makati itinerary keeps travel time short, letting you take your time and still cover it comfortably in half a day.
This is not a park but a cemetery where the war dead rest. Refrain from picnicking, jogging, exercising, bringing pets, loud noise, or playing music, and don't lean or climb on the headstones.
Drone photography isn't allowed without a permit. Commercial or group photography may also require prior authorization.
Avoid revealing clothing, and if a memorial ceremony is underway, watch quietly from a distance.
There's little shade across the grounds, so walking for a long time at midday carries a risk of heatstroke. Drink plenty of water.
